claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between coherent precipitate formation and retention of a disordered FCC solid solution.
The balance between coherent precipitates and a disordered FCC solid solution affects high-temperature strength.
The balance between coherent precipitates and a disordered FCC solid solution affects environmental resistance.
The balance between coherent precipitates and a disordered FCC solid solution affects radiation tolerance.
The balance between coherent precipitates and a disordered FCC solid solution affects cryogenic toughness.
Competition between precipitate formation and solid-solution retention influences dislocation mobility.
Competition between precipitate formation and solid-solution retention influences grain-boundary stability.
A higher fraction of coherent precipitates will improve high-temperature strength relative to a homogeneous disordered FCC baseline.
A higher fraction of coherent precipitates will improve environmental resistance relative to a homogeneous disordered FCC baseline.
A higher fraction of coherent precipitates will reduce cryogenic toughness relative to a homogeneous disordered FCC baseline.
A more stable disordered FCC solid solution will improve radiation tolerance.
A more stable disordered FCC solid solution will improve cryogenic toughness.
A more stable disordered FCC solid solution will reduce high-temperature strength.
The proposed hypothesis is bounded to 300–1000 K and strain rates of 10^-4–10^0 s^-1.
The proposed compositional domain is 5–20 at.% Al, 10–30 at.% Co, 10–30 at.% Cr, 20–40 at.% Fe, and 10–20 at.% Ni.
In situ TEM and synchrotron X-ray diffraction can be used to measure phase-transformation behavior during mechanical loading.
